k: After Alexander, Iran was ruled first by Greek kings, then for almost five centuries by the Parthian horse-archers, and then for four more by the Sasanians – the last great Iranian empire before Islam and Rome's most dangerous rival.

Long before Islam, Iranians followed the teachings of Zarathustra: one wise god, a cosmic struggle between truth and the lie, and fire as the sign of purity. The religion is small today, but its festivals, words and symbols are everywhere in Iranian life.

k: The Arab conquest brought Islam and Arabic to Iran, and for two centuries Persian was hardly written. Then, at the courts of the eastern dynasties, poets like Rudaki and Ferdowsi made it a great literary language again – one reason why Iranians, unlike Egyptians or Syrians, never switched to Arabic.

For some 1,500 years caravans carried silk, paper, spices and ideas between China and the Mediterranean – and almost every route ran through Iran. Iranians were the road's middlemen, and Persian was one of its languages.

In the 13th century the Mongols laid waste to Iran's great cities; within a few generations their descendants were building domes and observatories and patronising Persian poets. Timur repeated the terror a century later, and his heirs created one of the most brilliant courts in Persian history.
In 1501 a teenage Sufi leader made himself shah and Shi'ism the faith of Iran. A century later Shah Abbas the Great built a capital at Isfahan so splendid that people called it 'half the world'.

From the 1790s to 1925 the Qajar shahs ruled Iran from a new capital, Tehran. It was an age of lost wars and foreign pressure, but also of the first modern schools, newspapers and photographs – and of a protest movement that ended in revolution.

k: In 1906 Iranians forced their shah to accept a parliament and a constitution. The decades that followed brought oil, a new dynasty, rapid modernisation from above – and the 1953 coup that still shapes how Iranians see the West.

The 1979 revolution replaced the monarchy with an Islamic Republic. Since then Iran has lived through an eight-year war with Iraq, decades of sanctions and protest, and in 2026 a war with the United States and Israel.

The Persian you are learning is the language Darius carved on cliffs and Ferdowsi used for his Book of Kings. This is the thread that runs through 2,500 years of Iranian history, from cuneiform to Cyrillic.

k: Iran's sprawling capital climbs from the dry plain to the foot of the Alborz mountains. Palaces and a great bazaar in the south, mountain trails and tea houses in the north, and a metro that ties it all together.

k: Shah Abbas's capital of blue domes, arched bridges and one of the largest squares in the world. How to spend three days in 'half the world', what to eat there and when to go.
The city of Saadi and Hafez, of rose gardens, orange blossom and a mosque that fills with coloured light. What to see in Shiraz, what to eat, and how to hear the soft Shirazi accent.
A desert city of mud brick, windcatchers and underground water channels, and the heart of Iran's Zoroastrian community. What to see in Yazd, what to eat, and when to go.
An oasis town between the mountains and the desert, with the finest merchants' houses in Iran, the oldest surviving Persian garden and a spring festival of rosewater.

k: Iran's second city and its greatest place of pilgrimage, built around the shrine of Imam Reza – and the gateway to the tombs of Ferdowsi and Khayyam, to saffron fields and to the kebab houses of Shandiz.
A carpet and pistachio city on the edge of one of the hottest places on Earth, with a Safavid bazaar, a desert garden, the mud-brick citadel of Bam and the wind-carved ridges of the Lut.

Over the mountains from Tehran lies a different Iran: rain, rice paddies, tea gardens and ancient forests along the Caspian Sea. Rasht and its food, the stepped village of Masuleh, the Anzali lagoon and the roads north.
Hot, humid and open to the sea, Iran's south is a world apart. The port of Bandar Abbas, the rainbow island of Hormuz, the mangroves and canyons of Qeshm, and the holiday island of Kish.
In the Zagros mountains of western Iran, stepped villages cling to the slopes of the Hawraman valleys. Kurdish and Hawrami speech, the daf, a midwinter festival, mountain food and how to get there.

Two cities of the Zagros on the ancient road west: Hamadan, the old Median capital with the tombs of Avicenna and Baba Taher, and Kermanshah, where Achaemenid and Sasanian kings carved their deeds into the cliffs.
A visitor's guide to the heartland of the first Persian empire, north of Shiraz: the terraces of Persepolis, the royal tombs of Naqsh-e Rostam and the lonely tomb of Cyrus at Pasargadae.
Walls against the desert, water from the mountains, cypresses and a pavilion: the Persian garden gave the world the word 'paradise'. The idea behind it, and the nine gardens on UNESCO's list.
Persian was born as a literary language in the east, in the cities of Khorasan and Transoxiana. A journey to Herat, Bukhara and Samarkand – and how Dari and Tajik differ from the Persian of Iran.

Rice and slow-cooked stews, fresh herbs, a cloth spread on the floor and the old belief that every food is either 'hot' or 'cold': an introduction to how Iranians cook and eat, from the Caspian to the Persian Gulf.

Buttery saffron rice, a skewer of charcoal-grilled meat, a blistered tomato and a sprinkle of sumac: chelow kabab is the closest thing Iran has to a national dish. What goes into it, how it is grilled and how to order it.

k: A dark green stew of slow-fried herbs, lamb, kidney beans and dried limes, ghormeh sabzi is the dish many Iranians miss most when they are far from home.
Two stews every Iranian knows: gheymeh, with split peas, tomato and a crown of crisp potato straws, and fesenjan, dark and glossy with ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses.

k: Iranians cook rice with extraordinary care – soaked, boiled, drained and steamed into separate, fluffy grains – with a golden crust at the bottom of the pot that everyone wants a piece of.

k: Thick soups of herbs, beans and noodles, and a slow-cooked lamb broth that is eaten in two courses: ash and abgoosht are the hearty, old-fashioned heart of Iranian home cooking.

k: Herbs, broad beans, barberries, orange peel, sour cherries: Iranians mix almost anything into rice. A tour of the great polo dishes, from everyday lubia polo to jewelled wedding rice.
Iranian cooking is full of vegetables: herb-packed kuku, smoky aubergine from the Caspian, stuffed vine leaves, and cool yoghurt dishes said to be named after a queen.
Sangak baked on hot pebbles, ridged golden barbari, paper-thin lavash and soft taftun: bread is Iran's oldest staple, bought fresh every day from the neighbourhood bakery.
Strong, clear and amber-red, served in small glasses with a lump of sugar: tea is Iran's everyday drink, poured from a teapot that sits on top of a bubbling samovar.

k: Almost every Iranian city has a sweet it is famous for, from Isfahan's gaz to Qom's sohan. Add saffron rice pudding, rosewater sorbet and saffron ice cream, and you have a sweet tooth's map of Iran.

From the sweet wheat pudding on the haft-sin to herb rice with fish on New Year's Eve and pomegranates on the longest night of the year: the foods of the two great family nights of the Iranian calendar.
Iranian food is fragrant rather than fiery. Its spice box holds saffron, the 'red gold' of Khorasan, sour dried limes, turmeric for every stew and the rose-scented mixture called advieh.
Kebab houses and carpeted teahouses, busy cafés and street carts selling beetroot and broad beans – plus the art of ta'arof at the table and the polite battle over who pays.
Iran is a garden of fruit: pomegranates from Saveh, pistachios from Kerman, summer melons, sour green plums, fruit leather and the bowls of nuts and seeds that are set before every guest.

k: Nowruz, the 'new day', begins the Iranian year at the spring equinox. Weeks of cleaning and shopping lead up to one exact moment around the haft-sin table – followed by two weeks of visits, eydi and sweets.

k: From the formal proposal over a tray of tea to the sofreh-ye aghd with its mirror, candles and sugar cones, and a party that dances past midnight: how Iranians get married, step by step.

Tied by hand, one knot at a time, the Persian carpet is Iran's best-known art. How a carpet is woven, the two knots, the great weaving towns from Tabriz to Kerman, the nomads' gabbeh – and how to read the motifs.

k: Small, brilliant and made to be read together with poetry, Persian miniatures are among the great paintings of the world. Meet the Herat school and Behzad, the Tabriz masterpiece made for Shah Tahmasp, and Reza Abbasi's Isfahan.

In Iran, beautiful writing is the most honoured art of all. From angular Kufic and clear Naskh to Nastaliq, 'the bride of scripts', and racing Shekasteh – plus the reed pen, the ink and the black practice page.

k: Iwans and domes that lift the spirit, windcatchers, qanats and ice houses that beat the desert heat, and bridges built for strolling: a short guide to reading an Iranian building.
Persian classical music is poetry set free: a repertoire of melodies called the radif, twelve modal families, a handful of beautiful instruments – and great singers such as Mohammad-Reza Shajarian.

From popular melodramas to the New Wave, from Kiarostami's winding roads to Farhadi's family dramas, Iranian cinema has become one of the most admired in the world – at home and, more and more, abroad.

k: In Iran poetry is not only for books: people take omens from Hafez, paint verses on walls and trucks, play verse-capping games on winter nights and drop a well-chosen line into ordinary conversation.

k: Mosaics of wood and bone, enamel the colour of the sky, shimmering termeh and hand-printed cotton, copper beaten in the bazaar and pottery as old as Iran itself: a tour of the country's handicrafts.

Ferdowsi's Book of Kings is Iran's national epic: tyrants and blacksmiths, a magic bird, the hero Rostam and the tragedies of fathers and sons – told in a Persian that Iranians can still read, and acted out by storytellers in tea houses.

In a dry land a garden is paradise – and the word 'paradise' itself is Persian. The four-part chahar bagh, singing water and mirror-like pools, cypress and shade, and the nine gardens that UNESCO calls 'The Persian Garden'.

Does this dish have meat in it?
Do you have this in another colour?
fa: این را رنگ دیگری هم دارید؟
r: in rā rang-e digar-i ham dārid?

ti: Do you have a bigger size?
Can you give me a discount?
I'll give you two hundred thousand tomans.
OK, I'll think about it and come back.
Half a kilo of pistachios, please.
If it doesn't fit, will you take it back?
Thank you – sorry to impose on you.
Not at all – you're very welcome.
Shall I take my shoes off here?
Just a little something for you.
Thank you very much, I won't, thanks.
I'm full – honestly, it's not ta'ārof.
Where are you off to? It's still early!
You must come and visit us too.
fa: شما هم به ما سر بزنید.
r: shomā ham be mā sar be-zanid.

ti: I think I have food poisoning.
Do you have something for a cold?
How many times a day should I take it?
Do you have a tourist SIM?
How much is a data package?
Where can I charge my phone?
fa: کجا می‌توانم گوشی‌ام را شارژ کنم؟
r: kojā mi-tavānam gushi-am rā shārzh konam?

fa: ببخشید، صدایتان قطع و وصل می‌شود.
r: be-bakhshid, sedā-yetān ghat' o vasl mi-shavad.

ti: Give me your number. (to a friend)
Send me a voice message. (to a friend)
Give me a call. (to a friend)
Is it going to rain tomorrow?
Yes, very much! The people are so kind.
fa: بله، خیلی! مردمش خیلی مهربان هستند.
r: bale, kheyli! mardom-ash kheyli mehrabān hastand.

ti: How long have you been in Iran?
fa: چند وقت است در ایران هستید؟
r: chand vaght ast dar Irān hastid?

ti: Where have you been so far?
What are you up to these days? (to a friend)

fa: دلم برای خانواده‌ام تنگ شده است.
r: del-am barā-ye khānevāde-am tang shode ast.

ti: I'd love to go to Yazd.

fa: به نظر من خیلی خوب است.
r: be nazar-e man kheyli khub ast.

ti: I like it. / I love it.
I don't like it at all.
May you see a hundred more years like this!
Oh no – I hope it's nothing serious!
May harm stay far away from you!
I hope you get well soon.
fa: ان شاء الله زودتر خوب شوید.
r: en shā' allāh zud-tar khub shavid.

ti: May this be your last sorrow.
Excuse me, teacher, I have a question.
What's the difference between these two words?
Please write it on the board.
I'll teach you English and you teach me Persian.
fa: من به شما انگلیسی یاد می‌دهم، شما به من فارسی.
r: man be shomā engelisi yād mi-daham, shomā be man fārsi.

ti: Your Persian has got really good! (to a friend)
thank you (for what you've done for me)
well done; thank you for your hard work
thank you, dear; you're so kind
I'm so sorry for your loss
how wonderful for you! (on a happy arrival)
a guest is a gift from God
I doubt it; I don't think it'll happen

fa: دلش مثل سیر و سرکه می‌جوشد.
r: del-ash mesl-e sir o serke mi-jushad.

ti: to cheat someone, rip someone off
I've told you a thousand times
someone who makes more fuss than the person it concerns
blamed for something you didn't do
that's how it is – take it or leave it
fa: همین آش است و همین کاسه.
r: hamin āsh ast o hamin kāse.

ti: you're stuck with it either way
fa: آش کشک خاله‌ات است؛ بخوری پایت است، نخوری هم پایت است.
r: āsh-e kashk-e khāle-at ast; bo-khori pā-yat ast, na-khori ham pā-yat ast.

ti: to bite the hand that feeds you
talk is cheap; wishing won't make it so
fa: با حلوا حلوا گفتن دهان شیرین نمی‌شود.
r: bā halvā halvā goftan dahān shirin nemi-shavad.

ti: you've made your bed, now lie in it
fa: خربزه خوردی، پای لرزش هم بنشین.
r: kharboze khordi, pā-ye larz-ash ham be-neshin.

fa: هر چه بگندد نمکش می‌زنند، وای به روزی که بگندد نمک.
r: har che be-gandad namak-ash mi-zanand, vāy be ruz-i ke be-gandad namak.

ti: he's very shrewd; nothing gets past him
the whole story, from A to Z
too many cooks spoil the broth
fa: آشپز که دو تا شد، آش یا شور می‌شود یا بی‌نمک.
r: āshpaz ke do tā shod, āsh yā shur mi-shavad yā bi-namak.

ti: a bad penny always turns up; nothing ever happens to a rascal
it fell right into my lap; a piece of cake
a solution that keeps both sides happy
a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
fa: سرکه‌ی نقد به از حلوای نسیه.
r: serke-ye naghd beh az halvā-ye nesiye.

ti: every little helps; little by little it adds up
fa: قطره قطره جمع گردد، وانگهی دریا شود.
r: ghatre ghatre jam' gardad, vāngahi daryā shavad.

ti: with patience, the sour turns sweet
fa: گر صبر کنی، ز غوره حلوا سازی.
r: gar sabr koni, ze ghure halvā sāzi.

ti: slow and steady wins the race
fa: رهرو آن است که آهسته و پیوسته رود.
r: rahrow ān ast ke āheste o peyvaste ravad.

ti: play for time – something may turn up
fa: از این ستون به آن ستون فرج است.
r: az in sotun be ān sotun faraj ast.

ti: don't count your chickens before they're hatched

fa: ماهی را هر وقت از آب بگیری، تازه است.
r: māhi rā har vaght az āb be-giri, tāze ast.

ti: God helps those who help themselves
fa: از تو حرکت، از خدا برکت.
r: az to harekat, az khodā barekat.

ti: anything worth having has its price
fa: هر که طاووس خواهد، جور هندوستان کشد.
r: har ke tāvus khāhad, jowr-e hendustān keshad.

fa: کار نیکو کردن از پر کردن است.
r: kār-e niku kardan az por kardan ast.

ti: you can't do it alone; it takes teamwork
to undermine someone behind their back
to have connections, friends in high places
the more you have, the more you have to worry about
fa: هر که بامش بیش، برفش بیشتر.
r: har ke bām-ash bish, barf-ash bish-tar.

ti: cut your coat according to your cloth; live within your means
fa: پایت را به اندازه‌ی گلیمت دراز کن.
r: pā-yat rā be andāze-ye gelim-at derāz kon.

fa: جلوی ضرر را از هر جا بگیری، منفعت است.
r: jelow-ye zarar rā az har jā be-giri, manfa'at ast.

ti: you get what you pay for

fa: تعارف کم کن و بر مبلغ افزا.
r: ta'ārof kam kon o bar mablagh afzā.

ti: talk of the devil!; he's the image of his uncle

fa: مادر را ببین، دختر را بگیر.
r: mādar rā be-bin, dokhtar rā be-gir.

ti: don't take a couple's quarrels seriously
fa: زن و شوهر دعوا کنند، ابلهان باور کنند.
r: zan o showhar da'vā konand, ablahān bāvar konand.

fa: خدا در و تخته را خوب با هم جور کرده.
r: khodā dar o takhte rā khub bā ham jur karde.

ti: a little distance keeps a friendship sweet
it's a small world; we'll meet again
fa: کوه به کوه نمی‌رسد، آدم به آدم می‌رسد.
r: kuh be kuh nemi-resad, ādam be ādam mi-resad.

ti: a friend in need is a friend indeed
fa: دوست آن باشد که گیرد دست دوست، در پریشان‌حالی و درماندگی.
r: dust ān bāshad ke girad dast-e dust, dar parishān-hāli o darmāndegi.

ti: help that does more harm than good
birds of a feather flock together
fa: کبوتر با کبوتر، باز با باز، کند هم‌جنس با هم‌جنس پرواز.
r: kabutar bā kabutar, bāz bā bāz, konad ham-jens bā ham-jens parvāz.

ti: out of sight, out of mind
fa: از دل برود هر آن که از دیده برفت.
r: az del be-ravad har ān ke az dide be-raft.

ti: great minds think alike; the feeling is mutual
give him an inch and he'll take a mile
you didn't see anything – keep it to yourself
to blow a story out of all proportion
a loose tongue can cost you your head
fa: زبان سرخ سر سبز می‌دهد بر باد.
r: zabān-e sorkh sar-e sabz mi-dahad bar bād.

ti: say little, but make it count
fa: کم گوی و گزیده گوی چون دُر.
r: kam guy o gozide guy chon dorr.

ti: what comes from the heart goes to the heart
fa: سخن کز دل برآید، لاجرم بر دل نشیند.
r: sokhan k-az del bar-āyad, lājaram bar del neshinad.

fa: دیوار موش دارد، موش هم گوش دارد.
r: divār mush dārad, mush ham gush dārad.

ti: in for a penny, in for a pound
fa: آب که از سر گذشت، چه یک وجب چه صد وجب.
r: āb ke az sar gozasht, che yek vajab che sad vajab.

ti: the grass is always greener on the other side
anything can happen; don't be so sure
fa: سیب را که بالا بیندازی، تا پایین بیاید هزار چرخ می‌خورد.
r: sib rā ke bālā biyandāzi, tā pāyin biyāyad hezār charkh mi-khorad.

ti: you can tell from the start how it will go
fa: سالی که نکوست، از بهارش پیداست.
r: sāl-i ke neku-st, az bahār-ash peydā-st.

ti: wait and see how it ends
all that glitters is not gold

fa: تا نباشد چیزکی، مردم نگویند چیزها.
r: tā na-bāshad chizak-i, mardom na-guyand chiz-hā.

fa: مارگزیده از ریسمان سیاه و سفید می‌ترسد.
r: mār-gazide az rismān-e siyāh o sefid mi-tarsad.

ti: people show what they really are
fa: از کوزه همان برون تراود که در اوست.
r: az kuze hamān borun tarāvad ke dar u-st.

ti: strike while the iron is hot
fa: تا تنور گرم است، باید نان را چسباند.
r: tā tanur garm ast, bāyad nān rā chasbānd.

ti: where there's a will, there's a way

fa: توانا بود هر که دانا بود.
r: tavānā bovad har ke dānā bovad.

ti: dig a pit for others and you'll fall into it yourself

fa: سری که درد نمی‌کند، دستمال نمی‌بندند.
r: sar-i ke dard nemi-konad, dastmāl nemi-bandand.

fa: از هر دست بدهی، از همان دست پس می‌گیری.
r: az har dast be-dahi, az hamān dast pas mi-giri.

ti: judge yourself before you judge others
fa: یک سوزن به خودت بزن، یک جوالدوز به مردم.
r: yek suzan be khod-at be-zan, yek javāldoz be mardom.

ti: to kill two birds with one stone
fa: با یک تیر دو نشان زدن
r: bā yek tir do neshān zadan

ti: it's too late now; what's done is done
never put off till tomorrow what you can do today
fa: کار امروز را به فردا مینداز.
r: kār-e emruz rā be fardā mayandāz.

ti: when in Rome, do as the Romans do
fa: خواهی نشوی رسوا، هم‌رنگ جماعت شو.
r: khāhi na-shavi rosvā, ham-rang-e jamā'at show.

ti: a leopard can't change its spots
a sly one; a dark horse

fa: یکی به نعل می‌زند، یکی به میخ.
r: yek-i be na'l mi-zanad, yek-i be mikh.

ti: and he still has the nerve to complain
fa: دو قورت و نیمش هم باقی است.
r: do ghort o nim-ash ham bāghi ast.

ti: he wants to have his cake and eat it
fa: هم خدا را می‌خواهد، هم خرما را.
r: ham khodā rā mi-khāhad, ham khormā rā.

ti: big promises mean nothing will be done
to have no comeback; to give up
you only die once – let's get it over with
fa: مرگ یک بار، شیون یک بار.
r: marg yek bār, shivan yek bār.

ti: nothing to lose – it's worth a try
I've had enough; I can't take any more
nothing happened; nobody batted an eyelid
to dash someone's hopes; to give a final no
fa: آب پاکی را روی دست کسی ریختن
r: āb-e pāki rā ru-ye dast-e kas-i rikhtan

ti: to be shown up, made to look a fool
to do great damage for a small gain
fa: به خاطر یک دستمال، قیصریه را آتش زدن
r: be khāter-e yek dastmāl, gheysariye rā ātash zadan

fa: خودم کردم که لعنت بر خودم باد.
r: khod-am kardam ke la'nat bar khod-am bād.

ti: to spoil someone's fun; to put someone in their place
we never had any luck anyway
fa: خر ما از کرگی دم نداشت.
r: khar-e mā az korregi dam na-dāsht.

fa: خر بیار و باقالی بار کن.
r: khar biyār o bāghāli bār kon.

fa: گربه دستش به گوشت نمی‌رسد، می‌گوید بو می‌دهد.
r: gorbe dast-ash be gusht nemi-resad, mi-guyad bu mi-dahad.

ti: the pot calling the kettle black
fa: دیگ به دیگ می‌گوید رویت سیاه.
r: dig be dig mi-guyad ru-yat siyāh.

ti: he's longing for the old days

fa: اول چاه را بکن، بعد منار را بدزد.
r: avval chāh rā be-kan, ba'd menār rā be-dozd.

ti: if it's free, I'll take it

fa: آفتابه‌لگن هفت دست، شام و ناهار هیچ.
r: āftābe-lagan haft dast, shām o nāhār hich.

ti: to read; to sing; to study
to hit, strike; to play (an instrument)
to know (a person or place), recognise
to rain, snow (to fall, of rain or snow)
to turn (a corner); to twist, wrap
to command; (polite) to say, come, do
to pull; to draw; to smoke
to pass, go by; to cross
to wander, go around; to search
to deliver; to give someone a lift
to take out, take off; to earn
to give back, return; to translate
to do (formal for کردن); to seem
to get on, get in (a vehicle); to ride
to get off, get out (of a vehicle)
to finish, end; to run out
to collect, gather; to tidy up
to reduce, turn down; to take away
to keep, hold; to stop (a car)
to arrange to meet, make a date
to set off; to get going
to try hard, make an effort
to move; to set off, depart
to exist; there is, there are
to come to terms (with); to get along (with)
